correctness.rationale: For a quadratic steepest-descent step, Armijo is exactly the scalar constraint \(\alpha q\le2(1-\sigma)\). The squared new-gradient ratio is \(1-2t+Kt^2\), where the sharp condition-number-only moment factor is \(K\le(\kappa+1)^2/(4\kappa)\). Convexity in \(t\) places the supremum at the zero-step limit or the Armijo endpoint. The endpoint spectral construction attains the unsafe branch and can be scaled so an arbitrary prescribed first trial is accepted at equality. The rational witness and algebraic identities are replayed by the packaged checker.

originality.rationale: Classical Armijo sufficient decrease and classical exact-line-search gradient-norm oscillation are treated as prior work. The inspected Armijo source states objective monotonicity but not a gradient-norm condition-number frontier. The inspected full exact-line-search source gives the \(3+2\sqrt2\) threshold for exact line search but does not include the Armijo parameter or characterize all sufficient-decrease-admissible steps. Targeted database and literature searches found no implication-equivalent \(\sigma\)-dependent frontier or first-trial sharpness construction.
residual_risks: Older line-search literature is extensive, and an equivalent result may be phrased as a Kantorovich bound for sufficient-decrease steepest descent rather than as a gradient-norm safety frontier.
Adding Wolfe curvature conditions can exclude the sharp long Armijo step, so the theorem should not be transferred to Wolfe line searches without a fresh analysis.
The theorem is exact for quadratics; nonquadratic strongly convex functions can have changing Hessian geometry along the accepted segment.

value.rationale: Armijo sufficient decrease is a standard line-search acceptance rule, while the gradient norm is a standard stopping diagnostic. The theorem gives the exact point at which the acceptance rule ceases to protect that diagnostic, shows that the failure can occur on the very first accepted backtracking trial, and quantifies the effect by a sharp two-parameter law rather than a generic norm-equivalence estimate.
